name: Tomas Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't linked to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Riverside Drinks, the bottling plant on the north side, the one that makes juice and fizzy drinks for the supermarkets. I run the filler and the labeller on line four. That means I set it up for each product, keep an eye on the fill levels, clear jams when a bottle falls, and swap the label reels. On a good day we do about forty thousand bottles. I've been there six years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the team on line four, we've got a good crew and we have a laugh. The pay is better than most places, especially with overtime in summer. What wears me out is the changeovers, when we switch from orange to cola and have to clean everything. My fiancée Ana and I are getting married next September, so right now my head is full of seating plans. I've used an AI app for that, actually, it's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what most of us expected, a useful tool but not a big deal. I might joke about it with the guys on the line. I don't really post stuff online, except photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, nothing. My job is on the floor, and the floor doesn't care about chatbots. It'd be good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my shifts, take the summer overtime, and put it towards the wedding. Then start saving for a house with Ana. We've got about a year's costs saved already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even. It means we can just get on with our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding. Would anything change in your plans in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Wedding in September, small house by 2028, maybe kids after. Same plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Riverside change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planning office gets faster at scheduling changeovers. That would help me, actually, fewer surprise switches at the end of a shift.

say: AI would be a **useful tool**, not a big deal.
I'd joke about it with the **guys on the line**, not post online.
think: My job is on the **floor**, and chatbots don't touch it.
A plateau would be **good news** for us.
do: Work summer **overtime** and put it towards the wedding.
Start saving for a **house** with Ana afterwards.
Keep my shifts on **line four** as normal.
feel: **Calm**, even **happy**, free to get on with life.
S0.quote: My job is on the floor, and the floor doesn't care about chatbots.
fieldNote: His life is organised around the **wedding** next September.
He sees the plateau as **permission** to keep his plans.
He uses AI casually, for the **seating plan**, but not at work.

steps.text: Work summer overtime at Riverside to pay for the wedding
Marry Ana next September and save for a small house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change happens, you adapt. People said the same about computers. I'd say that at work if anyone got worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm OK for a while, but Ana's not. She books appointments and answers the phone at a dental practice, which is exactly the list on the card. If her job shrinks, our house plan slows down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, of course. I'd save harder, maybe put the overtime straight into savings instead of the wedding fund. And I'd tell Ana to start looking at what else she could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ana works on a dental reception desk. Does that change how you see this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Totally. A robot isn't coming for my job, a computer is coming for my fiancée's job. That's the part I hadn't thought about before you read it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use new tools at Riverside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others on the line were using it, yes. When they put in the new touchscreen on the labeller, I watched Kasia for a week and then I was fine. Same with this.

say: Change happens and **you adapt**, like with computers.
I'd calm people down at work if they got **worked up**.
think: I'm OK for a while, but **Ana's** reception job is on the card's list.
If her job shrinks, our **house plan** slows down.
do: Put summer **overtime** into savings, not the wedding fund.
Encourage Ana to look at **other work**.
Learn new line tools after **colleagues** try them.
S1.quote: A robot isn't coming for my job, a computer is coming for my fiancée's job.
fieldNote: The scenario hits his **fiancée's desk job** before his own.
He's surprised by this; it **reframes** the risk for him.
He learns new tools by **watching colleagues** first.

steps.text: Move summer overtime pay from the wedding fund into savings
Learn the new line software after colleagues try it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's way too fast and the government needs a plan, now. People can't just be thrown out. I'd probably share stuff about that online for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Ana's job goes in 2028 and mine goes around 2031, when the robots come. A bottling line is about as robot-friendly as it gets. We'd be thirty-one with no jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course as an industrial electrician next year. Somebody has to wire and install all these robots, at least for a few years. We'd shrink the wedding and put the house on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. My stomach goes tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married. But small, maybe forty people, not a hundred and twenty. The rest of the money stays in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Rui is an electrician, and he's never been out of work. Plants will need electricians while they install robots. It's the most sensible thing I can think of that uses my hands.

say: It's **too fast**, and the government needs a plan now.
People can't just be **thrown out**, and I'd post about it for once.
think: Ana's job goes in **2028** and mine around **2031**.
A **bottling line** is about as robot-friendly as it gets.
do: Start an evening course as an **industrial electrician** next year.
Cut the wedding to about **forty guests** and save the rest.
S2.quote: A bottling line is about as robot-friendly as it gets.
fieldNote: Both household jobs are at risk, Ana's **first** and his **second**.
His uncle, an electrician, makes **electrical work** feel like a safe bet.
Even so, the **wedding** still happens, just smaller.

steps.text: Start an evening industrial electrician course next year
Shrink the wedding to about forty guests
Put the house purchase on hold
Keep the leftover wedding money in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a bit of time but not much, so people should start planning now. Companies should have to help with retraining. I'd say that if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until about 2034 on the line, so around eight years. Ana's job goes earlier, maybe 2031. That's enough time to sort things out, but not enough to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the wedding as planned, but cheaper. Look at the electrician course in a year or two, once I've seen whether it works out for people. And keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a slower worry, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the electrician course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not straight away. I'd see if the first people from Riverside who did the electrician course got jobs, and then I'd start. If they did, I'd start in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller than we wanted. Something we could pay with one wage, just in case.

say: There's some **time** but not much, so people should plan now.
Companies should have to **help with retraining**.
think: I'd have about **eight years** on the line, until 2034.
That's enough to sort things out, but **not to relax**.
do: Hold the wedding as planned, but **cheaper**.
Start the **electrician course** in 2028 if others find work.
Buy a **smaller house** that one wage can pay for.
S3.quote: I'd see if the first people from Riverside who did the electrician course got jobs, and then I'd start.
fieldNote: More time brings back his habit of **waiting for proof**.
His **house plan** is resized to one wage as insurance.
He gives Ana's earlier risk equal weight in his **household** plans.

steps.text: Start the electrician course in 2028 if Riverside colleagues find work
Buy a smaller house that one wage can cover
Keep saving each month after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready. No need to panic. I'd say people should start learning new things slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots on my line around 2039 means I'd be forty. Ana's job would go around 2036. That's a long time from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job. Get married, buy the house, start a family. Around 2030 I'd think about the electrician course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If we waited for the world to be safe, nobody would have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to start thinking about what she'd like to do after reception, with no rush. Maybe dental nursing, which is more hands-on. We'd have time to work it out together.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** to get ready.
People should start **learning new things** slowly, without panic.
think: Robots reach my line around **2039**, when I'm forty.
Ana's reception job would go around **2036**.
That all feels like **a long time** from now.
do: Get married, buy the **house** and start a family.
Keep working on **line four** at Riverside.
S4.quote: If we waited for the world to be safe, nobody would have kids.
fieldNote: The long runway lets him put **family** first without hesitation.
He'd suggest Ana move to more **hands-on** dental nursing.
His retraining plan is **deferred**, not dropped.

steps.text: Marry Ana, buy the house and start a family
Keep working the filler and labeller on line four
Look at the electrician course around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Ana and I both go, one after the other, before we've even got a house. What would help is cheap evening courses for trades that are still needed, and some help with the mortgage if you lose your job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but our plans depend on two jobs. My fiancée Ana's job at the dental practice goes first in almost all your pictures, and nobody thinks of receptionists.

headlineQuote: My fiancée Ana's job at the dental practice goes first in almost all your pictures, and nobody thinks of receptionists.
portrait: Tomas, 27, runs the **filler and labeller** on a bottling line and is marrying Ana next September.
He's practical and adapts once others prove things work, using AI for **small tasks**.
He realises his fiancée's **reception job** is more exposed than his own.
He's calm in a plateau, uneasy in steady change and **alarmed** by AGI in 2028.
His plan is an **electrician course**, timed by how much warning there is.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Ana lose their jobs before buying a house.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **evening courses** for trades still in demand.
**Mortgage help** for people who lose their jobs.
